gap: No result ChatGPT got turns idle draw into daily energy. The 24 V 6,000 W low-frequency split-phase units it recommended draw 77–80 W at idle with no load, which is 1.85–1.92 kWh a day, or about 72–75% of a 24 V 100 Ah (2.56 kWh) battery. That is before any appliance runs.
standout_why: I compared against these pages. The cited Sigineer APC6024D page lists 80 W idle and 3,000 W per 120 V leg, but it never turns idle draw into kWh per day or a share of the battery bank. ChatGPT's answer says a 6,000 W unit 'does not necessarily supply all 6,000W on one 120V leg' but gives no per-leg number and says nothing about idle draw. liveoffthegrid.com/specs/inverters lists idle watts only for 48 V units, has no 24 V split-phase model, gives no surge duration and no per-leg figure. ecosolarkits.com's guide says its 24 V split-phase models are sold out and gives no per-leg rating for any unit. Dealectric's own page covers only 48 V hybrids. The per-leg part of the finding is partly on the cited Sigineer page. Idle draw as daily energy, set side by side across the 24 V candidates, is on none of these pages.
decides: This changes the pick for a 24 V bank, which is usually small. On idle draw alone, a 6,000 W low-frequency unit drains most of a 2.56 kWh battery in a day. For a typical 24 V system the stronger picks are the smaller units: Sigineer APC3024D (37 W idle) or AIMS 4,000 W (52.5 W idle). A 6,000 W unit makes sense only if the buyer needs 240 V motor surge (18,000 W for 20 s) and will run it in power-saver mode (15 W Sigineer, 29 W Sun Gold). The per-leg figure confirms the same choice. Sigineer states its 6,000 W unit gives at most 3,000 W between each 120 V hot line and neutral. So a 120 V-only load list does not benefit from 6,000 W. It needs a unit whose 120 V leg covers its largest 120 V load.
